{{short description|Idea that a concept is ill-defined, and therefore cannot be discussed}}
[[file:Lokistone.jpg|thumb|The [[Snaptun stone]] has been identified as [[Loki]] with his lips stitched shut after the wager]]
'''Loki's wager''' is the insistence that because two or more categories exist as poles on a spectrum  with a grey area in the middle, the distinction between the two cannot be defined.

==The wager==
In the [[Prose Edda]] ({{lang|non|[[Skáldskaparmál]]}} [[wikisource:Prose Edda/Skáldskaparmál#Loke.27s Wager With the Dwarves|ch. 35]]), the [[Norse mythology|Norse]] [[trickster]] god [[Loki]] made a bet with the dwarf [[Brokkr]] in which he wagered his head. Loki lost; when the dwarf came to collect it, Loki stated that he would relinquish his head, but noted that Brokkr was not entitled to any part of Loki's neck. After a discussion on the matter, while parts of Loki clearly belonged to the head ''or'' the neck, neither side could agree exactly where one ended and the other began. Loki therefore kept his head indefinitely,<ref name="Boudry">{{cite journal
|first=Maarten
|last=Boudry
|date=January 2014
|title=Loki's Wager and Laudan's Error: On Genuine and Territorial Demarcation
|url=https://philpapers.org/rec/BOULWA
|journal=Philosophy of Pseudoscience: Reconsidering the Demarcation Problem
|pages=79–98
|doi=10.7208/chicago/9780226051826.003.0006
|publisher=University of Chicago Press|url-access=subscription
}}</ref> though afterwards his lips were stitched shut by Brokkr as punishment for using tricky wordplay.<ref name="Guerber">{{cite book |last1=Guerber |first1=H. A. |title=Myths of the Norsemen From the Eddas and Sagas |date=1909 |publisher=George G. Harrap & Company |location=London |pages=59ff |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/28497/28497-h/28497-h.htm |access-date=7 January 2023 |chapter=4: Thor. Sif, the Golden-haired}}</ref> 

==In argumentation theory==
Loki's wager, therefore, is a situation in which a person unreasonably insists that a term cannot be defined, making it impossible to discuss.<ref name="Boudry" /> It has been described as a fallacy<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boudry |first=Maarten |date=2022 |title=Diagnosing Pseudoscience – by Getting Rid of the Demarcation Problem |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10838-021-09572-4 |journal=Journal for General Philosophy of Science |language=en |volume=53 |issue=2 |pages=83–101 |doi=10.1007/s10838-021-09572-4 |s2cid=240123249 |issn=0925-4560|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Dutton |first=Edward |url=https://www.doria.fi/bitstream/handle/10024/180296/WR-58%20Edward%20Dutton%20-%20Four%20Immigrant%20Churches%20and%20a%20Mosque.pdf |title=Four immigrant churches and a mosque: an overview of immigrant religious institutions in Oulu |publisher=Institute of Migration / Siirtolaisuusinstituutti |year=2009 |series=Web Reports 58 |pages=8}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Bennett |first=Bo |title=Loki's Wager |url=https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/questions/QNAs5YXP/lokis_wager.html |access-date=2023-11-10 |website=www.logicallyfallacious.com |language=en}}</ref> and more precisely as a kind of [[continuum fallacy]].<ref name=":0" />
